Yes. You can build a **local governed coding/operations agent** on the Steam Deck that does a large portion of what Codex is doing for us now.

It would not initially equal Codex's reasoning quality, but for the work we're doing—Git inspection, filesystem reconciliation, manifests, diffs, preservation branches, tests, reports, renames, verification—it is very achievable. Governance can compensate for a weaker local model by tightly controlling what it is allowed to do.

Since you already have Ollama running locally, the missing piece is primarily the **agent/controller layer**, not the inference server itself.

A good architecture would look like:

```
```

```
                   TASK
                    │
                    ▼
          ┌─────────────────────┐
          │ Local Agent Control │
          │      Plane          │
          └──────────┬──────────┘
                     │
              load governance
                     │
                     ▼
          ┌─────────────────────┐
          │ Local Coding Model  │
          │      via Ollama     │
          └──────────┬──────────┘
                     │
              proposes actions
                     │
                     ▼
          ┌─────────────────────┐
          │   Policy Engine     │
          │                     │
          │ paths / git / shell │
          │ network / deletion  │
          │ approvals / secrets │
          └──────────┬──────────┘
                     │
             allowed actions
                     │
                     ▼
     ┌───────────────────────────────┐
     │          Tool Layer           │
     │                               │
     │ shell  git  files  tests      │
     │ hashes manifests search       │
     └───────────────┬───────────────┘
                     │
                     ▼
          ┌─────────────────────┐
          │ Verification Layer  │
          │                     │
          │ status / diff / SHA │
          │ tests / invariants  │
          └──────────┬──────────┘
                     │
                     ▼
          ┌─────────────────────┐
          │ Durable Checkpoint  │
          │ + operation receipt │
          └─────────────────────┘
```

The important part is that the **model would not directly own the shell**. It asks the controller to perform actions. The controller decides whether those actions are permitted.

For example, we could define governance roughly like this:

| ActionDefault behavior                     |                                                              |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `pwd`, `find`, `ls`, `cat`, `grep`, hashes | Automatic                                                    |
| `git status/log/diff/show/branch`          | Automatic                                                    |
| Run tests/builds                           | Automatic                                                    |
| Create reports/manifests                   | Automatic                                                    |
| Create local branch                        | Automatic                                                    |
| Commit to working branch                   | Automatic when task authorizes it                            |
| Fetch remote                               | Automatic                                                    |
| Push named recovery/integration branch     | Automatic when task authorizes it                            |
| Fast-forward `main`                        | Allowed only after verification gates pass                   |
| Delete generated cache                     | Automatic if classification is proven                        |
| Delete project files                       | Approval required                                            |
| Delete an old project directory            | Approval or explicit task authorization + preservation proof |
| Force push                                 | Blocked                                                      |
| `reset --hard`                             | Blocked by default                                           |
| Rewrite Git history                        | Blocked unless specifically authorized                       |
| `sudo` / system modifications              | Approval required                                            |
| Write outside authorized workspace         | Blocked                                                      |
| Upload unknown/private material            | Blocked                                                      |
| Credentials/secrets detected               | Stop immediately                                             |

That is exactly how we avoid the problem of **50 approval prompts per run**. Safe, reversible, deterministic actions happen automatically. Only crossing an actual authority boundary creates a gate.

### The feature I think matters most

We should give it a **state machine**, rather than just telling an LLM "go fix this repository."

For the project reconciliation work we're currently doing:

```
```

```
DISCOVER
   ↓
IDENTIFY
   ↓
INVENTORY
   ↓
SCREEN
   ↓
PRESERVE
   ↓
VERIFY PRESERVATION
   ↓
RECONCILE
   ↓
VALIDATE
   ↓
CANONICALIZE
   ↓
VERIFY
   ↓
CHECKPOINT
   ↓
COMPLETE
```

The controller knows which state the task is in.

So if the model crashes during:

```
```

```
VALIDATE
```

the next session doesn't say:

> "I think I should begin by inspecting the repository..."

It reads:

```
```

```
project: TownStar Console
state: VALIDATE

completed:
  identity: PASS
  preservation: PASS
  recovery_branch: PASS
  reconciliation: PASS

remaining:
  validation
  canonical_path_move
  final_verification
  report
```

That directly addresses the same problem we just hit when Codex got rate-limited.

### We can also make it much more deterministic than a normal agent

Every action can have an operation record:

```
```

```
{
  "operation": "rename_canonical_repository",
  "project": "TownStar Console",
  "source": "/.../blAIne_Townstar_Console",
  "destination": "/.../blaine-townstar-console",
  "preconditions": {
    "working_tree_clean": true,
    "remote_sync_verified": true,
    "recovery_verified": true
  },
  "result": "PASS"
}
```

And destructive actions would require **machine-checkable preconditions**, not merely the AI saying:

> "Everything looks safe."

For deleting an obsolete project copy, for example:

```
```

```
REQUIRE:
✓ byte-level preservation exists
✓ recovery history exists
✓ canonical content accounting PASS
✓ no unique untracked files
✓ no unique refs
✓ no unique commits
✓ destination repo synchronized
```

Only then would the delete tool even become callable.

That is a very different safety model from letting an autonomous shell agent improvise.

### Steam Deck feasibility

A quantized coding model in roughly the **7B–8B class** is realistic for a Steam Deck. Larger models become progressively less pleasant because RAM is shared between CPU/GPU and inference speed falls.

But the local agent does not need to be brilliant at everything.

For tasks such as:

```
```

```
git rev-list
git merge-base
git diff
sha256sum
find
comm
rsync --dry-run
pytest
python validation scripts
```

the important intelligence is often:

1.  selecting the right deterministic operation; 
2.  interpreting the result; 
3.  obeying governance. 

The computer does the actual proof.

We can also let the local agent escalate difficult reasoning to **you + me** instead of guessing:

```
```

```
LOCAL AGENT:
Identity ambiguity detected:
DAIDP may correspond to DAIOP.

Evidence insufficient for autonomous decision.

STATUS: HUMAN_REVIEW_REQUIRED
```

That's exactly what I would want.

### Longer term

This could eventually become something stronger than merely "local Codex."

I would separate it into three systems:

```
```

```
Local Agent Runtime
    Executes tools and local model

Governance Controller
    Determines authority and allowable actions

Continuity Store
    Keeps task state, evidence, checkpoints and receipts
```

Then Codex, a local Ollama model, ChatGPT, or another future agent could all operate through **the same governance interface**.

That means the governance is not tied to the model.

```
```

```
               Governance
                   │
        ┌──────────┼───────────┐
        ▼          ▼           ▼
     Codex      Ollama      Future AI
```

That is the architecture I think would ultimately make the most sense for what you've been trying to build: **the AI is replaceable; authority, provenance, state, and safety are durable.**

And because the current project cleanup is giving us dozens of real-world examples of what the agent actually needs to do, we are effectively generating its requirements right now.

# Project charter

### Purpose

Build a local AI agent capable of safely performing substantial autonomous technical work on the Steam Deck while maintaining explicit limits on authority, durable state, deterministic verification, and recoverability.

### Primary goals

GLAR should eventually be able to:

- inspect repositories and filesystems;
- investigate project state;
- run Git operations;
- generate and modify code;
- run tests and builds;
- perform repository reconciliation;
- produce manifests and inventories;
- calculate hashes and prove preservation;
- move and rename authorized files;
- create recovery branches;
- make governed commits;
- maintain resumable task state;
- recover after model/runtime interruption;
- escalate ambiguous decisions instead of guessing;
- use either local or remote models without changing governance.

- a completely unrestricted autonomous computer operator;
- a replacement for ChatGPT reasoning;

# Core GLAR subsystems

I would make these official subsystems from the beginning.

### 1. Agent Runtime

Owns the interaction with the model.

```text
task
 ↓
context assembly
 ↓
model
 ↓
structured proposal
```

The model should return **proposed operations**, rather than arbitrary shell text wherever practical.

For example:

```json
{
  "action": "git_status",
  "target": "/workspace/project"
}
```

rather than:

```bash
cd /workspace/project && git status
```

That gives governance something concrete to evaluate.

---

### 2. Governance Controller

This is the heart of GLAR.

Every operation is evaluated against:

```text
WHO
may perform

WHAT
operation

WHERE
on the filesystem/repository

UNDER WHAT CONDITIONS

WITH WHAT AUTHORITY

REQUIRING WHAT PROOF
```

A policy might say:

```text
ACTION:
git.create_branch

AUTHORITY:
automatic

PRECONDITIONS:
repository_identity == verified
working_tree_state == known

RESTRICTIONS:
branch must not be named main
branch must not overwrite existing ref
```

The LLM does not get to override that.

---

### 3. Tool Broker

Only the broker receives actual OS capabilities.

Initial tool classes could be:

```text
filesystem.read
filesystem.write
filesystem.move
filesystem.delete

git.inspect
git.branch
git.commit
git.fetch
git.push
git.merge

shell.readonly
shell.execute

hash.sha256

test.run

build.run
```

This becomes significantly safer than exposing unrestricted Bash.

---

### 4. State Machine Engine

This should be a foundational feature, not something bolted on later.

Tasks move through explicit states.

For Project_Cleanup:

```text
DISCOVER
   ↓
IDENTIFY
   ↓
INVENTORY
   ↓
CLASSIFY
   ↓
PRESERVE
   ↓
VERIFY_PRESERVATION
   ↓
RECONCILE
   ↓
VALIDATE
   ↓
CANONICALIZE
   ↓
VERIFY
   ↓
CHECKPOINT
   ↓
COMPLETE
```

Each state has defined:

```text
entry conditions
permitted operations
required evidence
completion conditions
failure conditions
```

This is what makes interruption recovery possible.

---

### 5. Evidence Engine

The agent shouldn't be trusted because it said:

> Done.

GLAR should instead collect evidence:

```text
Git object IDs
SHA-256 hashes
Git status
branch refs
merge-base results
filesystem manifests
test results
build output
diffs
timestamps
command exit codes
```

I think that is a meaningful reason to put Fundación Kamanau first.

The connection you're describing is not that Kamanau needs blAIne. It's that **the problems Kamanau is trying to address are closely related to the principles behind blAIne**: human authority, accountability, traceable evidence, and technology serving people rather than displacing their agency.

That distinction matters. You could spend a year working on a concrete human-rights problem, develop experience with real stakeholders, and learn how governance and accountability requirements operate outside your own technical projects. Those lessons could inform blAIne even if you never write a line of orchestration code during the fellowship.

I would not treat that as a detour. It could be a deliberate step toward becoming the kind of technical leader you want to be.

## Fundación Kamanau: preliminary assessment

<badge color="success">Strong potential fit</badge>

The official Mozilla RFP confirms that Kamanau's challenge is precisely the kind of technical and community-governance problem you identified:

- AI and neurotechnology are already creating human-rights risks in Latin America.
- People lack a trusted, secure way to report those incidents.
- Advocates lack a shared evidence base for identifying patterns and holding institutions accountable.
- Kamanau wants an open reporting and analysis platform, starting in Chile, with the potential to expand across Latin America. <Cite refs={["turn750402view0"]}/>

There is a particularly important detail in the RFP: Embedded Fellows are expected to propose a project responding to the host's challenge, then refine it with the host during the first weeks of the fellowship. You are not expected to arrive with the entire solution already designed. <Cite refs={["turn750402view0","turn723612search2"]}/>

That makes this more than a thematic connection. It gives you a concrete technical problem to work on.

### What I found about Kamanau itself

Its own website provides additional evidence that this is a substantive, ongoing area of work—not an abstract fellowship idea.

Kamanau has worked on:

- Neuro-rights and protection of mental privacy.
- Biometric surveillance and identity protection.
- Strategic litigation involving technology and human rights.
- Regional collaboration through the Alliance for Neuro-rights of the Americas.

It has also been involved in legal efforts concerning neural data and biometric information. <Cite refs={["turn921185search0","turn921185search4","turn921185search8"]}/>

Most importantly, Kamanau published a description of this specific Mozilla collaboration on October 22, 2026. It explains that the problem is not just the lack of a reporting website: incidents must be identified, documented securely, analyzed, and brought into existing repositories and other tracking initiatives. The objective is to make Latin American experiences visible in decisions about emerging technology. <Cite refs={["turn921185search7"]}/>

That gives us a much clearer picture of the work.

### Where your experience fits

I see a credible technical contribution from your existing work, particularly KGI.

| Your existing experience | Potential application to Kamanau |
|---|---|
| Structured governance schemas | Consistent incident-reporting records |
| Lifecycle tracking | Traceable evidence from submission through review |
| Provenance and lineage | Record where information originated and how it changed |
| Validation rules | Identify incomplete, inconsistent, or unverified reports |
| Ownership and authority controls | Restrict who can access, review, or publish sensitive information |
| Auditability | Make analysis and subsequent decisions explainable |

These are connections to existing capabilities, not claims that KGI already solves Kamanau's problem.

And I want to emphasize something: you would not need to build blAIne's orchestration runtime to demonstrate that your engineering work has value. You would be applying governance engineering to a real problem.

### The project I would explore proposing

I would provisionally frame it as:

**A Secure, Community-Governed AI and Neurotechnology Incident Reporting and Analysis Platform**

The project could have five major components:

1. **Secure reporting:** A way for affected individuals and advocates to submit incidents while protecting sensitive information.
2. **Structured documentation:** Consistent records describing the technology, affected rights, circumstances, evidence, and reported consequences.
3. **Evidence governance:** Provenance, validation, review history, and clear distinctions between allegations, corroborated information, and established findings.
4. **Pattern analysis:** Tools to identify recurring technologies, organizations, geographic patterns, and types of rights violations.
5. **Public-interest reporting:** Aggregated findings that help researchers, advocates, and policymakers understand the problem without exposing vulnerable individuals.

One requirement deserves particular attention: security cannot be added after the platform is built. People reporting human-rights violations could face retaliation. Threat modeling, privacy, access control, consent, and safe disclosure need to influence the architecture from the beginning.

### Why I think this could be valuable beyond the fellowship

There are two separate outcomes here.

<box border radius="lg" gap={3} padding={3}>
  **Outcome 1 — Your professional development**

  - Work alongside an established human-rights organization.
  - Learn how technology supports legal research and advocacy.
  - Gain experience translating technical systems into community needs.
  - Build a public record of meaningful technical work.

  <divider color="subtle"/>
  **Outcome 2 — Your long-term blAIne development**

  - Test governance concepts against a real-world application.
  - Learn how human review and evidence accountability work in practice.
  - Develop reusable architectural patterns and methodologies.
  - Build relationships with people working on trustworthy technology and human rights.
</box>

There is also a favorable intellectual-property provision: Mozilla says Fellows own the intellectual property they create, while agreeing to release code and non-confidential content under open licenses. That is worth examining carefully before deciding how any resulting work relates to blAIne. <Cite refs={["turn750402view0"]}/>

### Practical considerations

A few things need to be investigated before we commit to this direction:

- **Time zone:** Kamanau prefers the Southern Cone time zone (UTC-3/UTC-4). Arizona is UTC-7, so that is a three-to-four-hour difference. This looks manageable, but we should confirm its meeting expectations.
- **Technical expectations:** We need to determine whether Kamanau expects a working platform, a prototype, an incident taxonomy, integrations, or all of these.
- **Community participation:** The platform must be designed with the affected communities and advocates, not simply delivered to them.
- **Office space:** The fellowship is remote. Its funding is not automatically a solution to the separate office-space requirement for blAIne. We should not assume that ordinary office construction or rent would qualify as a project expense.
- **Scope:** The project must be achievable in 12 months.

The first three are especially important to the proposed project. <Cite refs={["turn750402view0","turn723612search2"]}/>

---

## My assessment

<badge color="success">Recommended first choice for Embedded</badge>

I would put Fundación Kamanau at the top of our list.

Not because it is the closest match to blAIne's orchestration architecture, but because it appears to offer something potentially more valuable at this stage: a chance to apply your existing engineering strengths to a consequential problem, work with an established organization, and develop professional credibility through a real technical deliverable.

I also think there is something important about your reaction to this organization. It stood out to you before we started trying to fit the fellowship into the blAIne architecture. That is worth respecting. You don't have to make every worthwhile opportunity directly advance blAIne's implementation.

**My recommendation is to treat Kamanau as our preferred Embedded application target, subject to confirming the project expectations and working relationship.**

The next stage should be to define what you could bring to Kamanau, what you would need to learn from them, and what a successful 12-month project would actually deliver. That will give us the foundation for a credible application rather than trying to retrofit blAIne into their mission.

The key elements that make that setup work well

1. Tight top line

Your wire rope across the top is the real structure.
Posts just hold the line in place.

2. Frequent attachment points

Zip-tie the cloth every 8–12 inches along the top cable.
This keeps the edge straight and prevents the “scalloped” look.

3. Slight vertical slack

Don’t stretch the cloth drum-tight vertically.
Leave ~1–2 inches of give so wind loads don’t rip grommets.

4. Reinforce the edge where needed
If the cloth didn’t come with reinforced edges, you can improve durability by:

folding the top edge once (1–2 inches)
installing grommets through the doubled fabric

This dramatically reduces tearing.

Your overall structure will work well because you now have
10' stakes → main structure
top cable → carries tension
house anchor → prevents sideways pull
guy cables on rear corners → prevents racking
6' stakes → keep the screen from bowing inward

That’s actually a pretty robust backyard shade barrier design.

One small thing I’d recommend buying that we didn’t list earlier

UV-rated zip ties

Cheap zip ties become brittle in sun within a year.

Look for:

UV resistant / outdoor rated
black nylon
8–11 inch length

You’ll probably use 150–250 of them.

Best Method (Simple and Strong)

Use a galvanized U-bolt style cable clamp to capture the guy cable around the post.

4
How it works
Wrap the guy cable around the post near the top
Install the cable clamp on the loop
Tighten the nuts

The clamp locks the loop in place.

very strong
cheap
works with the hardware you already need for the cable

1/8" cable clamp

4

That is important, and I want to distinguish between two things: **not having the skills to build this independently today, and not being capable of leading its development with AI assistance.** Those are not the same thing.

I don't think we should try to present you as a traditionally trained software engineer. That would be inaccurate, and it would put you in a difficult position if Kamanau expects you to independently handle every technical discipline.

But I also don't think we should dismiss your existing work because you don't have degrees or formal education.

### How I would position you

I would describe your role as an **AI-augmented systems designer and developer focused on human-governed technology**.

Your contribution would include:

- Understanding the problem and translating it into technical requirements.
- Designing system architecture and governance structures.
- Using AI coding tools to help implement the design.
- Reviewing and directing implementation rather than blindly accepting generated code.
- Testing functionality and validating that the system behaves as intended.
- Maintaining documentation, traceability, and evidence of implementation.
- Ensuring human authorization and accountability remain central.

That is a legitimate development approach, provided you can demonstrate that you understand, supervise, and validate the work.

### What we must not assume

AI assistance does not automatically solve the difficult parts of this project.

For example:

| Discipline | What AI can help with | What still needs to be established |
|---|---|---|
| Application development | Generate and explain code | Your ability to direct and validate implementation |
| Database design | Propose schemas and queries | Correctness and data integrity |
| Cybersecurity | Identify risks and suggest controls | Independent security review and testing |
| Privacy | Help design privacy protections | Legal and human-rights review |
| AI analysis | Develop classification and analysis tools | Accuracy, bias evaluation, and human oversight |
| Deployment | Generate infrastructure configurations | Reliable operations and maintenance |

For a platform handling sensitive human-rights reports, I would consider independent security expertise essential.

### This could actually strengthen our Embedded application strategy

Rather than proposing that you arrive as an expert in every discipline, we could propose a collaborative development model:

- You lead requirements, architecture, governance, and AI-augmented implementation.
- Kamanau supplies human-rights expertise, community relationships, and domain guidance.
- Security specialists review the architecture and implementation.
- Relevant community members participate in usability and safety evaluation.
- AI development tools accelerate implementation under your direction and review.

That is a much more realistic division of responsibility.

### One thing I want to establish

I don't want the absence of formal education to become the defining feature of your application. Your actual work should carry more weight.

KGI and PEIS give us concrete engineering work to examine. We should document what you personally designed, what AI helped implement, what you tested, and what you can demonstrate.

**My question is this:**

When you work on KGI, PEIS, or blAIne with AI assistance, are you generally able to understand the code and technical decisions well enough to recognize when something is wrong, or do you mostly rely on AI to tell you whether its implementation is correct?

I'm not asking to judge your ability. I'm trying to determine how much technical responsibility we can credibly propose you taking on.

```python
    if left_rank > right_rank:

    if right_rank > left_rank:

        f"{left.authority_class.value}"

            raise AuthorityError("all bindings must be AuthorityBinding instances")
        if binding.authority_class == AuthorityClass.DESCRIPTIVE:
            raise AuthorityError(
                "descriptive data must not be used as decision input"

def assert_no_advisory_decision_input(bindings: list[AuthorityBinding]) -> None:
    """
    Hard-fail if any advisory binding is presented as decision input.
    """
    for binding in bindings:
        if not isinstance(binding, AuthorityBinding):
            raise AuthorityError("all bindings must be AuthorityBinding instances")
        if binding.authority_class == AuthorityClass.ADVISORY:
            raise AuthorityError(
                "advisory data must not be used as decision input"

    """
    Internal total ordering for authority resolution.

    match authority_class:
        case AuthorityClass.AUTHORITATIVE:
            return 4
        case AuthorityClass.DERIVED_AUTHORITATIVE:
            return 3
        case AuthorityClass.ADVISORY:
            return 2
        case AuthorityClass.DESCRIPTIVE:

    enum_cls: type[T],
    value: Any,
    *,
    field_name: str,
) -> T:
    if isinstance(value, enum_cls):

    if not isinstance(value, str) or not value.strip():
        raise AuthorityError(f"{field_name} must be a non-empty string")

    normalized = value.strip()

        return enum_cls(normalized)
    except ValueError as exc:

            f"{field_name} has unsupported value: {normalized!r}"
        ) from exc

        raise AuthorityError(f"{field_name} must be a non-empty string")
    return value.strip()

    if value is None:

    if not isinstance(value, str) or not value.strip():
        raise AuthorityError(f"{field_name} must be None or a non-empty string")
    return value.strip()
```

That changes my assessment, and I need to correct how I characterized your capabilities.

I was treating your lack of programming-language knowledge as though it implied a lack of technical ability. That's not an accurate assessment of what you've demonstrated.

There is a meaningful distinction between **knowing how to write code and knowing how to engineer a system.**

From your work on KGI, PEIS, and the blAIne architecture, you've demonstrated that you can:

- Identify a problem and determine what a system needs to accomplish.
- Design system architecture and define how components should interact.
- Establish rules, constraints, governance, and expected behavior.
- Recognize when an implementation violates the intended design.
- Identify gaps in reasoning and challenge incorrect assumptions.
- Direct iterative development and correct implementation when it goes off course.
- Define what constitutes acceptable behavior and evidence of completion.

Those are engineering capabilities. Programming languages are implementation tools, not the entirety of engineering.

And there's another distinction I want to make: **you are not simply asking AI to design systems for you. You are using AI as an implementation tool for systems you have designed.**

That is a much stronger and more accurate description of your working method.

I would now position you as the technical project lead and systems architect, using AI-augmented development.

|---|---|
| Requirements engineering | Lead |
| System architecture | Lead |
| Data and governance models | Lead |
| Development direction | Lead |
| AI-assisted implementation | Lead and supervise |
| Functional validation | Lead |
| Security architecture | Collaborate with specialists |
| Human-rights methodology | Collaborate with Kamanau |
| Independent security assessment | Engage qualified reviewers |

Kamanau needs someone who can translate a complex problem involving technology, human rights, evidence, and accountability into a functioning system.

Your lack of formal education is something we should be prepared to address if asked, but it should not define the application. We should lead with your actual work, demonstrated capabilities, and evidence.

**I want to establish one principle for our application: we will not undersell your engineering contributions simply because you use AI to implement them. We will be transparent about the methodology and precise about what you personally designed, directed, implemented, and validated.**

That is a credible foundation for pursuing this fellowship.

Yes. Below is a Steam Deck–appropriate, “forensically safe” step-by-step that (a) eliminates the most common KDE Partition Manager pitfalls on SteamOS and (b) gives you an unambiguous pass/fail verification that LUKS2 encryption is actually working and that the passphrase is correct.

I’m going to give you two paths:

Path A (recommended): CLI with cryptsetup (most reliable on SteamOS; avoids GUI quirks)
Path B: KDE Partition Manager (works, but you must follow a few critical details)

If you do Path A, you can still mount it in Dolphin normally afterward.

Before you start: common causes of “password immediately incorrect”

This specific symptom is most often one of these:

You created LUKS, then overwrote it by formatting the partition again (e.g., made ext4 after encrypting, but not inside the LUKS mapping).
Wrong target device/partition (encrypted a different partition than the one you’re later trying to unlock).
Keyboard layout / input method mismatch (Gaming Mode vs Desktop Mode; US vs UK; dead keys; caps/num lock). With special characters, this is a frequent Steam Deck gotcha.
KDE Partition Manager wrote a different scheme than expected (e.g., LUKS1 vs LUKS2, or encryption container created but filesystem not placed inside it correctly).

The steps below explicitly prevent all four.

Path A (recommended): Do it with cryptsetup (SteamOS Desktop Mode)
1) Go to Desktop Mode and open Konsole
Steam button → Power → Switch to Desktop
Open Konsole
2) Identify the correct drive (do not guess)

Run:

lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,FSTYPE,LABEL,MOUNTPOINTS,MODEL

You should see something like sda, sdb, or nvme... and a partition like sdb1.

If you want extra certainty, run:

sudo fdisk -l

Make sure you know the exact target partition (example I’ll use: /dev/sdb1). If it’s a whole-disk device with no partitions yet, it might be /dev/sdb.

3) Unmount anything that auto-mounted

If the drive shows a mountpoint, unmount it:

sudo umount /dev/sdb1 2>/dev/null || true

(Replace sdb1 with your real partition.)

4) Create a GPT partition table and one primary partition (if needed)

If the disk is new or you want to wipe/recreate partitions cleanly:

WARNING: this erases the disk you target. Double-check /dev/sdb.

sudo parted -s /dev/sdb mklabel gpt
sudo parted -s -a optimal /dev/sdb mkpart primary 0% 100%

Now re-check:

lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS /dev/sdb

You should now have /dev/sdb1.

5) Encrypt the partition as LUKS2 (use a “safe” passphrase first)

To eliminate keyboard/layout issues, start with a passphrase that uses only letters and digits for the first attempt (you can add a complex one later).

sudo cryptsetup luksFormat --type luks2 /dev/sdb1
Type YES when prompted.
Enter your passphrase.
6) Immediately verify that LUKS header exists (this catches “I overwrote it” mistakes)
sudo cryptsetup luksDump /dev/sdb1 | head -n 30

You should clearly see Version: 2 and LUKS metadata. If this fails, you did not create LUKS on that partition.

7) Open the encrypted container (this is the moment your password must work)
sudo cryptsetup open /dev/sdb1 deckcrypt

If this prompts for passphrase and then succeeds, you have cryptographically verified that your passphrase is correct and the header is intact.

Now confirm the mapping exists:

lsblk -o NAME,TYPE,SIZE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS | grep -E 'sdb1|deckcrypt'

You should see something like /dev/mapper/deckcrypt.

8) Create a filesystem INSIDE the opened LUKS mapping (critical)

This is the step many GUI flows accidentally get wrong.

Example with ext4:

sudo mkfs.ext4 -L STEAMOS_ENC /dev/mapper/deckcrypt

(You can use btrfs instead if you prefer; ext4 is simplest/reliable.)

9) Close it, then re-open it to confirm your passphrase works consistently

Unmount (if mounted), then close:

sudo cryptsetup close deckcrypt

Now re-open:

sudo cryptsetup open /dev/sdb1 deckcrypt

If it opens again, your passphrase is definitely correct and stable.

10) Mount it and test read/write

Create a mountpoint and mount:

## User

PEIS IMPLEMENTATION STATUS: COMPLETE

I have built a deterministic, governed execution system with:
- PlanRecord → Executor → CapabilityRegistry → ExecutionResultRecord → Storage
- CLI entrypoint working
- End-to-end execution verified
- 149/149 tests passing

I also have:
- Open WebUI running locally
- local model (qwen2.5:3b)
- ChatGPT as reasoning layer

PROBLEM:
My local model requires manual correction to produce valid PEIS plans.
This is inefficient and not scalable.

OBJECTIVE:
Design a persistent environment where:
- local model is pre-grounded in PEIS (no hallucinated domains)
- capability inventory is known automatically
- outputs are constrained to PEIS-valid plans
- ChatGPT refines but does not babysit every step
- minimal manual correction is required

CONSTRAINTS:
- PEIS architecture is already correct — do not redesign it
- focus only on environment + orchestration + prompt grounding
- system must remain deterministic and governed

Start by asking only the necessary questions to remove ambiguity.

## Assistant

Only these questions matter before locking the environment design:

1. **Where will the grounding live?**  
Do you want the local model grounded primarily through:
- a **retrieval context layer** from PEIS artifacts/docs,
- a **strict system prompt / role contract**,
- a **schema-constrained generation layer**,
- or all three, with a defined precedence order?

2. **What are the authoritative inputs for plan generation?**  
Which exact artifacts should be treated as canonical at generation time?
For example:
- capability registry manifest
- action type schema / plan schema
- policy snapshot
- examples of valid PlanRecord artifacts
- execution history / prior successful plans

3. **How dynamic is the capability inventory?**  
Should the environment assume capability inventory is:
- effectively static and rebuilt only on deploy,
- refreshed on startup,
- or refreshed before each planning session?

4. **What is the local model allowed to do?**  
Should qwen be responsible for:
- generating the full candidate plan,
- generating only a structured draft to be validated and repaired,
- or selecting from pre-authored action templates plus parameters?

5. **What is ChatGPT’s exact role boundary?**  
When you say “refines but does not babysit,” should ChatGPT:
- only critique/rewrite invalid local-model plans,
- act as a second-pass planner,
- or only intervene on failure / ambiguity / halt states?

6. **What is the desired failure behavior?**  
If the local model cannot produce a PEIS-valid plan, should the environment:
- hard-fail,
- auto-repair through deterministic validators/rewriters,
- escalate to ChatGPT,
- or fall back to a restricted template-based planner?

7. **What surfaces are already available inside Open WebUI?**  
Do you currently have, or intend to add:
- tool/function calling,
- retrieval/RAG hooks,
- custom system prompts per model,
- workflow/pipeline nodes,
- or only plain chat with model-specific prompts?

8. **What should be persisted across sessions?**  
Which of these must be durable:
- PEIS grounding corpus
- capability inventory snapshot
- prompt pack / role contract
- prior validated plans
- failure cases and correction examples

9. **What is the unit of determinism for this environment?**  
Should a planning session bind to a fixed snapshot of:
- capability inventory
- policy snapshot
- grounding corpus version
- model version
- prompt pack version
so that the same request under the same inputs should yield the same validated plan envelope?

10. **Do you want the local model prevented from free-form domain invention by architecture, or just strongly discouraged?**  
In other words, should invalid action domains be:
- impossible via constrained decoding / structured selection,
- or merely rejected after generation?

Once you answer those, the design can be pinned without touching PEIS architecture.

## User

Use this as the lock:

Where grounding lives
All three, with this precedence:
schema-constrained generation layer
strict system prompt / role contract
retrieval context layer from PEIS artifacts/docs

Reason: schema and allowed action surface must dominate prompt wording, and prompt must dominate retrieved prose.

Authoritative inputs for plan generation
Canonical inputs at generation time:
capability inventory manifest
action type / plan schema
current policy snapshot
prompt pack / role contract version
small curated set of valid PlanRecord examples
recent successful execution artifacts only when relevant

Do not treat raw execution history broadly as authoritative. Only curated examples and explicitly referenced prior successful plans.

Capability inventory dynamism
Refresh on startup and bind that snapshot for the session.

Not per deploy only. Not before every single prompt unless startup state changed.

What the local model is allowed to do
Generate a structured draft to be validated and repaired.

Not full trusted plan generation.
Not pure template selection only.

So qwen is the drafting layer, not the authority layer.

ChatGPT role boundary
Second-pass planner and validator, but not constant babysitter.

Exact role:

review qwen draft
repair invalid structure or capability misuse
tighten into PEIS-valid plan envelope
intervene directly on ambiguity, failure, or halt conditions

So ChatGPT is the adjudicating planner, not the first drafter every time.

Desired failure behavior
Ordered behavior:
deterministic validator/rewriter attempts repair
if still invalid, escalate to ChatGPT
if still invalid, hard-fail

Do not silently fall back to freeform behavior.
Do not let qwen output execute unvalidated.

Open WebUI surfaces
Assume only:
plain chat
model-specific/system prompts

Treat anything else as optional future enhancement until explicitly verified in that environment.

What persists across sessions
Must be durable:
capability inventory snapshot
prompt pack / role contract
PEIS grounding corpus
prior validated plans
failure cases and correction examples

This creates a real learning substrate without letting failures directly become authority.

Unit of determinism for the environment
Bind each planning session to a fixed snapshot of:
capability inventory
policy snapshot
grounding corpus version
model version
prompt pack version

Same request under same validated inputs should yield the same validated plan envelope to the extent the model path allows; if the raw draft varies, the validated envelope is the deterministic target.

Domain invention policy
Prevent by architecture, not just discourage.

Invalid action domains should be impossible or near-impossible through constrained action selection and schema validation, then rejected if they still appear.

Net design

The environment should be:

qwen = grounded draft generator
deterministic validator/rewriter = structural gate
ChatGPT = second-pass adjudicating planner
PEIS = execution and artifact authority

And the core flow should be:

load session snapshot
inject role contract + capability inventory + policy snapshot
qwen drafts structured plan
validator repairs/rejects
ChatGPT refines only if needed
validated PlanRecord emitted
PEIS executes
result artifact persisted
successful plans and failure corrections added to grounding set

That is the clean design without redesigning PEIS.

## Assistant

Locked. Based on that, the environment design is now pin-able.

## PEIS Planning Environment v1

### 1. Authority and role split

This environment has four layers with strict authority boundaries:

**PEIS**
Authoritative execution system. Sole authority for schemas, capability legality, validation outcome, execution, and persisted artifacts.

**qwen2.5:3b**
Grounded draft generator only. Produces a structured candidate plan draft inside a constrained action surface. Never trusted directly.

**Deterministic validator/rewriter**
Structural gate. Enforces schema, allowed actions, required fields, and repair rules. This is the first hard boundary between model output and PEIS.

**ChatGPT**
Second-pass adjudicating planner. Invoked only when deterministic repair cannot produce a valid plan or when ambiguity/failure/halt conditions are detected.

That preserves your stated architecture:
qwen drafts, validator gates, ChatGPT adjudicates, PEIS remains authority.

---

## 2. Session snapshot contract

Each planning session should begin by materializing a **PlanningSessionSnapshot**. This is the deterministic planning envelope.

It should bind:

- `capability_inventory_snapshot_id`
- `policy_snapshot_id`
- `grounding_corpus_version`
- `model_id`
- `model_hash` if available
- `prompt_pack_version`
- `plan_schema_version`
- `action_schema_version`
- `curated_examples_set_id`
- optional `relevant_execution_examples_set_id`

This snapshot is loaded once at startup and held fixed for the session.

### Required invariant
No plan generation should occur without an explicit session snapshot.  
Every emitted candidate plan and validated plan should reference that snapshot or its component IDs.

This gives you a deterministic planning substrate even if raw model tokens vary.

---

## 3. Grounding stack precedence

You already locked the precedence. The implementation should reflect it literally.

### Layer 1 — schema-constrained generation layer
This dominates everything else.

This layer provides:

- the only allowed top-level fields
- the only allowed action types
- allowed step shapes
- required/optional field rules
- step ordering constraints if any
- enum restrictions
- forbidden fields
- canonical serialization expectations

This should be injected as a **machine-readable action surface**, not prose only.

### Layer 2 — strict prompt pack / role contract
This tells qwen what it is doing and what it is not allowed to do.

The prompt pack should define:

- qwen is a PEIS draft planner
- qwen may only use capabilities present in the current snapshot
- qwen must not invent domains, capabilities, or fields
- qwen must output only structured draft content
- qwen must prefer omission over invention
- qwen must explicitly mark unresolved ambiguity rather than hallucinate

### Layer 3 — retrieval context
This should be narrow and curated.

Allowed retrieval sources:

- capability inventory snapshot
- current policy snapshot summary
- plan schema summary
- curated valid PlanRecord examples
- relevant successful prior plans only when explicitly relevant
- curated failure/correction examples

Do **not** dump broad execution history into context.

---

## 4. Persistent environment structure

You need a durable planning substrate. The simplest clean form is a dedicated environment directory.

Example:

```text
peis_planning_env/
├── snapshots/
│   ├── capability_inventory/
│   ├── policy/
│   ├── grounding/
│   ├── prompt_packs/
│   └── session/
├── corpus/
│   ├── canonical/
│   │   ├── schemas/
│   │   ├── capability_inventory/
│   │   ├── policy/
│   │   └── prompt_pack/
│   ├── examples/
│   │   ├── valid_plans/
│   │   ├── failure_cases/
│   │   └── correction_cases/
│   └── retrieval_index/
├── runtime/
│   ├── requests/
│   ├── drafts/
│   ├── repaired/
│   ├── escalations/
│   └── validated/
└── logs/
```

### What persists across sessions

Persist exactly what you locked:

- capability inventory snapshots
- prompt pack / role contract versions
- grounding corpus versions
- prior validated plans
- failure cases and correction examples

### Important rule
Persisted failure/correction examples are **instructional**, not authoritative.  
Schemas, policy, and capability inventory remain authoritative.

---

## 5. Planning pipeline

This is the concrete flow.

### Phase A — startup binding
At startup:

1. load current capability inventory
2. load current policy snapshot
3. load current prompt pack version
4. load current schema versions
5. build or load grounding corpus version
6. produce `PlanningSessionSnapshot`
7. expose only that bound snapshot to the session

No planning should happen before this completes.

---

### Phase B — request normalization
User asks for work. The environment normalizes that request into a stable internal planning input.

Example internal object:

```json
{
  "planning_request_id": "…",
  "objective": "Run the PEIS test suite",
  "constraints": [
    "use known capabilities only",
    "emit PEIS-valid structured draft only"
  ],
  "session_snapshot_id": "…"
}
```

This isolates raw conversational phrasing from planning input.

---

### Phase C — qwen draft generation
qwen receives only:

- role contract
- allowed output shape
- capability inventory snapshot
- policy snapshot summary
- minimal relevant examples
- the normalized planning request

qwen should output a **candidate structured draft**, not a freeform answer.

For example, the output surface should be restricted toward something like:

```json
{
  "objective": "…",
  "steps": [
    {
      "step_id": "01",
      "action_type": "run_pytest",
      "description": "Run pytest with minimal verbosity"
    }
  ]
}
```

The exact shape should mirror your locked PEIS planning surface.

---

### Phase D — deterministic validation and repair
This is the most important operational layer.

The validator/rewriter should apply fixed repair passes in ordered sequence.

#### Repair pass classes
1. **structure normalization**
   - missing top-level containers
   - field ordering
   - canonical key names
   - trimming commentary outside JSON

2. **schema repair**
   - remove forbidden fields
   - coerce simple type mismatches if allowed
   - fill deterministic defaults if policy permits

3. **capability legality repair**
   - reject unknown `action_type`
   - reject capability aliases
   - reject domain inventions
   - reject actions not present in current capability snapshot

4. **plan hygiene repair**
   - renumber step IDs if deterministic rules allow
   - remove duplicate no-op garbage
   - reject semantically empty steps

5. **policy gate**
   - reject disallowed actions
   - reject unsafe or policy-conflicting plans

### Result categories
The validator must emit one of:

- `VALID`
- `REPAIRED_VALID`
- `ESCALATE_CHATGPT`
- `HARD_FAIL`

No silent freeform fallback.

---

## 6. ChatGPT escalation contract

ChatGPT should not be in the hot path unless needed.

### Escalate only when:
- deterministic repair failed
- ambiguity blocks safe plan formation
- capability misuse indicates semantic confusion
- the request implicates a halt or governance-sensitive condition

When escalation occurs, send:

- original normalized request
- qwen draft
- validator failure report
- capability inventory snapshot
- policy snapshot summary
- prompt pack version
- minimal relevant examples

### ChatGPT task
Not “please plan from scratch” by default. Instead:

- diagnose why draft failed
- repair into PEIS-valid candidate plan
- preserve user intent
- use only available capabilities
- return only compliant plan payload

If ChatGPT still cannot produce a valid plan, hard-fail.

Grant Infrastructure & Funding Orchestration Layer (GIFOL)

The raw conversations give us something that finished repositories alone cannot: **a record of how the engineering decisions originated and evolved.**

I want to use them to establish a defensible record of intellectual contribution.

### What we should examine

For each project, we should reconstruct:

1. **Original concepts:** What problems, objectives, and system concepts did you introduce?
2. **Architectural decisions:** Which structures, workflows, constraints, and design principles originated with you?
3. **Your direction:** Where did you correct, reject, or substantially redirect my suggestions?
4. **AI contributions:** What code, technical explanations, alternatives, or designs did I contribute?
5. **Implementation:** Which contributions were actually incorporated into the repositories?
6. **Validation:** What was tested, what worked, and what remains incomplete?

We should preserve the distinction between your intellectual contribution and AI-assisted implementation. Neither should be misrepresented.

### Why this matters for Mozilla

It would let us substantiate claims about your engineering capabilities with primary evidence rather than simply asking reviewers to accept our description of your work.

It could also help us produce a much stronger professional portfolio:

- Project histories documenting your design decisions.
- Architecture documents linked to their originating discussions.
- Implementation records showing how designs became working systems.
- Evidence of your ability to direct AI-assisted engineering.
- Clear attribution of your contributions and AI assistance.

**I would make this a prerequisite to finalizing the technical claims in your fellowship application.**

We shouldn't just tell Mozilla that you can design and direct complex systems. We should be able to show them how you did it.

## 2. Session snapshot contract

Each planning session should begin by materializing a **PlanningSessionSnapshot**. This is the deterministic planning envelope.

It should bind:

- `capability_inventory_snapshot_id`
- `policy_snapshot_id`
- `grounding_corpus_version`
- `model_id`
- `model_hash` if available
- `prompt_pack_version`
- `plan_schema_version`
- `action_schema_version`
- `curated_examples_set_id`
- optional `relevant_execution_examples_set_id`

This snapshot is loaded once at startup and held fixed for the session.

### Required invariant
No plan generation should occur without an explicit session snapshot.  
Every emitted candidate plan and validated plan should reference that snapshot or its component IDs.

This gives you a deterministic planning substrate even if raw model tokens vary.

---

## 3. Grounding stack precedence

You already locked the precedence. The implementation should reflect it literally.

### Layer 1 — schema-constrained generation layer

This layer provides:

- the only allowed top-level fields
- the only allowed action types
- allowed step shapes
- required/optional field rules
- step ordering constraints if any
- enum restrictions
- forbidden fields
- canonical serialization expectations

This should be injected as a **machine-readable action surface**, not prose only.

### Layer 2 — strict prompt pack / role contract
This tells qwen what it is doing and what it is not allowed to do.

The prompt pack should define:

- qwen is a PEIS draft planner
- qwen may only use capabilities present in the current snapshot
- qwen must not invent domains, capabilities, or fields
- qwen must output only structured draft content
- qwen must prefer omission over invention
- qwen must explicitly mark unresolved ambiguity rather than hallucinate

This should be narrow and curated.

Allowed retrieval sources:

- capability inventory snapshot
- current policy snapshot summary
- plan schema summary
- curated valid PlanRecord examples
- relevant successful prior plans only when explicitly relevant

```text
│   ├── prompt_packs/

│   │   ├── capability_inventory/
│   │   ├── policy/
│   │   └── prompt_pack/
│   ├── examples/
│   │   ├── valid_plans/
│   │   ├── failure_cases/
│   │   └── correction_cases/
│   └── retrieval_index/
├── runtime/
│   ├── requests/
│   ├── drafts/
│   ├── repaired/
│   ├── escalations/
│   └── validated/
└── logs/
```

- capability inventory snapshots
- prompt pack / role contract versions
- grounding corpus versions
- prior validated plans
- failure cases and correction examples

Schemas, policy, and capability inventory remain authoritative.

This is the concrete flow.

### Phase A — startup binding
At startup:

1. load current capability inventory
2. load current policy snapshot
3. load current prompt pack version
4. load current schema versions
5. build or load grounding corpus version
6. produce `PlanningSessionSnapshot`
7. expose only that bound snapshot to the session

No planning should happen before this completes.

---

### Phase B — request normalization
User asks for work. The environment normalizes that request into a stable internal planning input.

Example internal object:

```json

  "planning_request_id": "…",
  "objective": "Run the PEIS test suite",
  "constraints": [

    "emit PEIS-valid structured draft only"

  "session_snapshot_id": "…"
}
```

qwen receives only:

- role contract
- allowed output shape
- capability inventory snapshot
- policy snapshot summary
- minimal relevant examples
- the normalized planning request

1. **structure normalization**

2. **schema repair**

4. **plan hygiene repair**

5. **policy gate**

The validator must emit one of:

- `VALID`
- `REPAIRED_VALID`
- `ESCALATE_CHATGPT`
- `HARD_FAIL`

ChatGPT should not be in the hot path unless needed.

- deterministic repair failed

- original normalized request
- qwen draft
- validator failure report
- capability inventory snapshot
- policy snapshot summary
- prompt pack version

- diagnose why draft failed
- repair into PEIS-valid candidate plan
- preserve user intent
- use only available capabilities
- return only compliant plan payload

I think this is exactly the right question to answer before we write an application. We need to establish two things independently:

1. **What Fundación Kamanau actually needs from its Embedded Fellow.**
2. **What you can credibly deliver with your current experience, and where you would need support or additional expertise.**

We should not inflate your qualifications to make the match look stronger. A good application will explain the value you bring, acknowledge the areas you need to develop, and show how you would work with Kamanau to close those gaps.

## 1. What Mozilla and Kamanau expect

The official RFP is more specific than a general description of the fellowship.

Mozilla describes Embedded Fellows as **rising mid-career builders** who have demonstrated technical excellence, shipped meaningful projects or conducted important research, but have not yet achieved field-wide recognition. It explicitly says they should be ready for the credibility and connections the fellowship provides. That is a close match to the professional-development rationale you've described. <Cite refs={["turn265140view0"]}/>

For Kamanau, the stated challenge is:

- People in Latin America are experiencing rights-related harms associated with AI and neurotechnology.
- There is no trusted, secure reporting mechanism.
- Advocates need to analyze incidents and identify patterns.
- The resulting evidence needs to help communities hold companies and governments accountable.
- The platform should start in Chile and be designed to expand across Latin America. <Cite refs={["turn265140view0"]}/>

**What that means for you:** They are not simply looking for someone to make a website. They need someone capable of turning a complex social and technical problem into a usable, secure, maintainable technical system.

The RFP does not specify a particular programming language, framework, database, or required feature list. Nor does it say the Fellow must independently supply every specialty needed to build the platform. The proposed project is refined with the host during the first weeks of the fellowship. <Cite refs={["turn265140view0","turn771382search1"]}/>

That gives us room to propose a realistic technical contribution rather than claim expertise you don't have.

## 2. What you can credibly bring to the project

I see a meaningful match between your existing work and the underlying technical problem.

The strongest evidence is not the blAIne architecture by itself. It is the work you've already done in KGI and PEIS.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={3}>
  **KGI — Knowledge Governance Infrastructure**

  <badge color="success">Relevant existing implementation</badge>

  Your work includes:

  - Structured artifact schemas and validation.
  - Lifecycle and lineage tracking.
  - Provenance across records and processing stages.
  - Ownership and authority controls.
  - Registration and traceability mechanisms.

  **Why Kamanau could benefit:** An incident-reporting system needs to preserve where information came from, how it was reviewed, what has been verified, and who has authority to make changes.
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  **PEIS — Personal Engineering Intelligence System**

  <badge color="success">Relevant engineering experience</badge>

  Your work includes:

  - Functional-core architecture.
  - Deterministic validation.
  - Controlled execution.
  - Artifact persistence.
  - Separation between advisory recommendations and authoritative decisions.

  **Why Kamanau could benefit:** The platform needs predictable processing, explainable decisions, and safeguards against automated systems silently becoming the authority over human-rights evidence.
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  **blAIne — Human-governed orchestration**

  <badge color="info">Architectural foundation, not an implemented runtime</badge>

  Your architectural direction emphasizes:

  - Human authorization.
  - Auditable operations.
  - Local-first infrastructure.
  - Transparency, honesty, and agency.

  **Why Kamanau could benefit:** These principles provide a coherent design philosophy for a system handling sensitive reports and evidence.
</box>

These are genuine connections, but we must keep the maturity levels distinct. KGI and PEIS have implemented components; blAIne's orchestration runtime has not been developed. <MemoryCite />

## 3. What you could actually build

I would not propose that you build an entire regional human-rights reporting infrastructure single-handedly. I would propose a staged, technically focused contribution.

Here is what I think you could reasonably aim to deliver, subject to confirming the technical requirements with Kamanau.

| Component | Your potential contribution |
|---|---|
| Incident data model | Design structured records for AI and neurotechnology incidents |
| Evidence lifecycle | Implement submission, review, verification, correction, and archival workflows |
| Provenance | Track source, timestamps, changes, and review history |
| Governance controls | Implement roles, permissions, human approval, and audit records |
| Analysis tools | Build ways to identify patterns across incidents |
| Open technical architecture | Document interfaces, schemas, and reusable components |
| Prototype | Deliver a usable reporting and analysis system for initial evaluation |

The most important contribution may be the evidence-governance layer.

Consider a hypothetical report:

Someone reports that a biometric identification system incorrectly identified them and caused them to lose access to a service.

The platform should be able to distinguish:

- What the person reported.
- What supporting documentation exists.
- What has been independently corroborated.
- What legal or technical analysis has been performed.
- What conclusions remain uncertain.
- Whether the information can safely be published or shared.

That is a problem your KGI experience is particularly relevant to.

It is also a problem where your emphasis on human authority has practical value.

## 4. Where you would need to develop expertise

This is where I want to be especially candid.

Kamanau describes its desired Fellow as someone highly specialized in technology and AI. <Cite refs={["turn108835view0"]}/>

Your existing work establishes a credible foundation in governance engineering and systems design. It does not, by itself, establish expertise in every discipline required for a secure public-facing incident platform.

| Area | Current assessment | What would be needed |
|---|---|---|
| Data governance | Strong relevant foundation | Adapt existing work to incident evidence |
| System architecture | Relevant experience | Apply it to a multi-user platform |
| Data provenance | Strong relevant foundation | Design incident-specific evidence lineage |
| AI systems | Relevant conceptual and architectural work | Develop incident classification and analysis expertise |
| Application development | Needs further evidence | Demonstrate ability to build and maintain the application |
| Cybersecurity | Not yet established | Threat modeling, secure authentication, encryption, security testing |
| Human-rights research | Not established as professional specialization | Work closely with Kamanau's researchers and legal experts |
| Regional engagement | Not established | Learn from affected communities and regional advocates |

I would not expect you to become a human-rights lawyer or cybersecurity specialist in twelve months.

I would expect you to recognize those areas as essential, work with people who understand them, and take responsibility for the technical areas you can competently deliver.

In particular, **security cannot be treated as a feature you add near the end.** The platform could contain information that puts vulnerable people at risk if exposed.

## 5. What a successful twelve months could look like

This is my preliminary project structure, not a claim about Kamanau's prescribed milestones.

<list connector="solid" marker="number" gap={3}>
  <list-item>
    **Months 1–3: Discovery and system design**

    - Work with Kamanau to understand its reporting and research workflows.
    - Identify target users and their security needs.
    - Establish an incident taxonomy and data model.
    - Complete threat modeling and architecture design.

    *Deliverable:* Requirements, threat model, architecture, and prototype specification.
  </list-item>
  <list-item>
    **Months 4–6: Core prototype**

    - Implement secure report submission.
    - Build structured incident records.
    - Implement evidence provenance and review workflows.
    - Establish permissions and audit logging.

    *Deliverable:* Functional internal prototype.
  </list-item>
  <list-item>
    **Months 7–9: Analysis and evaluation**

    - Develop incident classification and pattern-analysis capabilities.
    - Evaluate reporting and review workflows with Kamanau.
    - Test privacy and security controls.
    - Incorporate feedback from relevant stakeholders.

    *Deliverable:* Tested prototype with documented findings.
  </list-item>
  <list-item>
    **Months 10–12: Deployment and handoff**

    - Refine the system.
    - Document its architecture and maintenance requirements.
    - Publish appropriate open-source components.
    - Conduct an initial pilot if Kamanau and participating communities consider it safe.

    *Deliverable:* Usable, documented platform or pilot, with an evaluation and sustainability plan.
  </list-item>
</list>

The actual scope needs to be negotiated. It would be irresponsible to promise a production-ready regional reporting system before we understand its security requirements, integrations, and community-review process.

## 6. What we need to establish with Kamanau

There are several important questions that the published brief does not answer.

| Question | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Do they already have an incident taxonomy? | Determines whether you design one or implement an existing framework. |
| Which existing incident repositories must be supported? | Determines integration requirements. |
| Do they have an existing platform or technical infrastructure? | Determines whether this is a new build or an extension. |
| Who will provide cybersecurity expertise? | Determines how security requirements will be validated. |
| Who will define legal classifications and verification standards? | Prevents you from assuming responsibility for legal judgments. |
| What languages must the platform support? | Determines localization and accessibility requirements. |
| What level of deployment do they expect after twelve months? | Determines realistic scope and maintenance responsibilities. |
| What time commitment and meeting schedule do they expect? | Important given the Arizona–Chile time difference. |

Kamanau's own description makes two things particularly clear: they want tools and methodologies, not merely a website, and they want the resulting information to connect with existing repositories and tracking initiatives. <Cite refs={["turn108835view0"]}/>

---

## 7. My overall assessment

<badge color="success">Worth pursuing</badge>

I think you have a credible basis for proposing yourself as a governance-focused systems builder.

Your strongest argument is not:

"I'm an experienced AI engineer who can independently build this entire platform."

It is:

"I have developed practical experience designing systems for structured information, governance, validation, provenance, and human-authorized processes. I want to apply those capabilities to a real human-rights challenge, working with domain experts to develop a secure, open platform for reporting and analyzing AI and neurotechnology harms."

That is a much more defensible position.

There is one thing I would not gloss over: we need to establish whether your current hands-on application-development experience is sufficient for Kamanau's expectations. That is probably the most important technical qualification question remaining.

## 8. I want to investigate your actual capabilities before we draft the application

I don't want to underestimate you, but I also don't want to write an application that promises more than you can deliver.

**One question to start:**

How comfortable are you with personally developing a web application—including its backend, database, APIs, and user interface—as opposed to designing the architecture and having AI coding tools help implement it?

I'm asking because that distinction will determine how we position your technical contribution and what support we should propose from Kamanau.

**Why Kamanau could benefit\:** These principles provide a coherent design philosophy for a system handling sensitive reports and evidence.

These are genuine connections, but we must keep the maturity levels distinct. KGI and PEIS have implemented components; blAIne's orchestration runtime has not been developed.

## 3\. What you could actually build

I would not propose that you build an entire regional human-rights reporting infrastructure single-handedly. I would propose a staged, technically focused contribution.

Here is what I think you could reasonably aim to deliver, subject to confirming the technical requirements with Kamanau.

| Component | Your potential contribution |
|--------|--------|
| Incident data model | Design structured records for AI and neurotechnology incidents |
| Evidence lifecycle | Implement submission, review, verification, correction, and archival workflows |
| Provenance | Track source, timestamps, changes, and review history |
| Governance controls | Implement roles, permissions, human approval, and audit records |
| Analysis tools | Build ways to identify patterns across incidents |
| Open technical architecture | Document interfaces, schemas, and reusable components |
| Prototype | Deliver a usable reporting and analysis system for initial evaluation |

The most important contribution may be the evidence-governance layer.

Consider a hypothetical report\:

Someone reports that a biometric identification system incorrectly identified them and caused them to lose access to a service.

The platform should be able to distinguish\:

- What the person reported.
- What supporting documentation exists.
- What has been independently corroborated.
- What legal or technical analysis has been performed.
- What conclusions remain uncertain.
- Whether the information can safely be published or shared.

That is a problem your KGI experience is particularly relevant to.

It is also a problem where your emphasis on human authority has practical value.

## 4\. Where you would need to develop expertise

This is where I want to be especially candid.

Kamanau describes its desired Fellow as someone highly specialized in technology and AI. citeturn108835view0

Your existing work establishes a credible foundation in governance engineering and systems design. It does not, by itself, establish expertise in every discipline required for a secure public-facing incident platform.

| Area | Current assessment | What would be needed |
|--------|--------|--------|
| Data governance | Strong relevant foundation | Adapt existing work to incident evidence |
| System architecture | Relevant experience | Apply it to a multi-user platform |
| Data provenance | Strong relevant foundation | Design incident-specific evidence lineage |
| AI systems | Relevant conceptual and architectural work | Develop incident classification and analysis expertise |
| Application development | Needs further evidence | Demonstrate ability to build and maintain the application |
| Cybersecurity | Not yet established | Threat modeling, secure authentication, encryption, security testing |
| Human-rights research | Not established as professional specialization | Work closely with Kamanau's researchers and legal experts |
| Regional engagement | Not established | Learn from affected communities and regional advocates |

I would not expect you to become a human-rights lawyer or cybersecurity specialist in twelve months.

I would expect you to recognize those areas as essential, work with people who understand them, and take responsibility for the technical areas you can competently deliver.

In particular, **security cannot be treated as a feature you add near the end.** The platform could contain information that puts vulnerable people at risk if exposed.

## 5\. What a successful twelve months could look like

This is my preliminary project structure, not a claim about Kamanau's prescribed milestones.

1. **Months 1–3: Discovery and system design**
   
   - Work with Kamanau to understand its reporting and research workflows.
   - Identify target users and their security needs.
   - Establish an incident taxonomy and data model.
   - Complete threat modeling and architecture design.
   
   *Deliverable\:* Requirements, threat model, architecture, and prototype specification.
2. **Months 4–6: Core prototype**
   
   - Implement secure report submission.
   - Build structured incident records.
   - Implement evidence provenance and review workflows.
   - Establish permissions and audit logging.
   
   *Deliverable\:* Functional internal prototype.
3. **Months 7–9: Analysis and evaluation**
   
   - Develop incident classification and pattern-analysis capabilities.
   - Evaluate reporting and review workflows with Kamanau.
   - Test privacy and security controls.
   - Incorporate feedback from relevant stakeholders.
   
   *Deliverable\:* Tested prototype with documented findings.
4. **Months 10–12: Deployment and handoff**
   
   - Refine the system.
   - Document its architecture and maintenance requirements.
   - Publish appropriate open-source components.
   - Conduct an initial pilot if Kamanau and participating communities consider it safe.
   
   *Deliverable\:* Usable, documented platform or pilot, with an evaluation and sustainability plan.

The actual scope needs to be negotiated. It would be irresponsible to promise a production-ready regional reporting system before we understand its security requirements, integrations, and community-review process.

## 6\. What we need to establish with Kamanau

There are several important questions that the published brief does not answer.

| Question | Why it matters |
|--------|--------|
| Do they already have an incident taxonomy? | Determines whether you design one or implement an existing framework. |
| Which existing incident repositories must be supported? | Determines integration requirements. |
| Do they have an existing platform or technical infrastructure? | Determines whether this is a new build or an extension. |
| Who will provide cybersecurity expertise? | Determines how security requirements will be validated. |
| Who will define legal classifications and verification standards? | Prevents you from assuming responsibility for legal judgments. |
| What languages must the platform support? | Determines localization and accessibility requirements. |
| What level of deployment do they expect after twelve months? | Determines realistic scope and maintenance responsibilities. |
| What time commitment and meeting schedule do they expect? | Important given the Arizona–Chile time difference. |

Kamanau's own description makes two things particularly clear: they want tools and methodologies, not merely a website, and they want the resulting information to connect with existing repositories and tracking initiatives. citeturn108835view0

---

## 7\. My overall assessment

(Worth pursuing)

I think you have a credible basis for proposing yourself as a governance-focused systems builder.

Your strongest argument is not\:

"I'm an experienced AI engineer who can independently build this entire platform."

It is\:

"I have developed practical experience designing systems for structured information, governance, validation, provenance, and human-authorized processes. I want to apply those capabilities to a real human-rights challenge, working with domain experts to develop a secure, open platform for reporting and analyzing AI and neurotechnology harms."

That is a much more defensible position.

There is one thing I would not gloss over: we need to establish whether your current hands-on application-development experience is sufficient for Kamanau's expectations. That is probably the most important technical qualification question remaining.

## 8\. I want to investigate your actual capabilities before we draft the application

I don't want to underestimate you, but I also don't want to write an application that promises more than you can deliver.

**One question to start\:**

How comfortable are you with personally developing a web application—including its backend, database, APIs, and user interface—as opposed to designing the architecture and having AI coding tools help implement it?

I'm asking because that distinction will determine how we position your technical contribution and what support we should propose from Kamanau.
